name: Duke of Wellington Statue
description: An equestrian bronze of Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, seated on his real Waterloo warhorse Copenhagen and gesturing firmly east toward Waterloo Place. Sculpted by Sir John Steell, who won the commission in 1842, it was unveiled on 18 June 1852, the 37th anniversary of the Battle of Waterloo, and stands directly in front of General Register House at the eastern end of Princes Street.
interesting_fact: Wellington himself, then 83 and in his final months, did not attend the unveiling, but surviving veterans of his campaigns turned out for the ceremony. Copenhagen, the horse, was entirely real: Wellington rode him throughout the Waterloo campaign and kept him in retirement afterwards until he died in 1836, aged 28, and was buried with full military honours. In mid-2026 the statue started turning up in the news for an unwanted reason - spotted wearing a traffic cone, copying a decades-old Glasgow tradition around that city's own Wellington statue after Tartan Army fans crowned statues abroad during the World Cup, a trend Edinburgh councillors have publicly called 'undignified'.
source_notes: No dedicated Wikipedia article exists for this statue (only the Hyde Park Corner and Glasgow Wellington statues have their own pages); facts drawn from Canmore/Historic Environment Scotland and corroborated across Edinburgh Expert and tourism sources. Google Places attributes it a Waterloo Place address rather than Princes Street - kept since coordinates match the statue's known position in front of Register House exactly. Traffic-cone trend confirmed as a genuine, dated mid-2026 news story (Edinburgh Evening News/Street Historians coverage), explicitly distinguished there from Glasgow's much older, unrelated cone tradition - not conflating the two statues.

name: General Register House
description: A grand neoclassical building designed by Robert Adam, its foundation stone laid on 27 June 1774 as purpose-built home for Scotland's national archives - reputedly the first building anywhere in Britain or Ireland constructed specifically to store public records. Money ran out repeatedly and it wasn't fully finished until 1834, sixty years after it began. At its heart sits the Adam Dome, a 50-foot-wide rotunda lit only by a central oculus, modelled on Rome's Pantheon.
interesting_fact: Adam worked small carved thistles into the dome's otherwise thoroughly Roman-inspired anthemion frieze, a quiet Scottish signature in an imported classical language. The building still does the job it was built for nearly 250 years later, holding centuries of Scotland's birth, marriage, death and court records, and remains the seat of the Lord Clerk Register and Lord Lyon King of Arms. It was actually judged too small before it was even finished - later architects Robert Reid and Archibald Elliot were called back in to extend it and dig further storage into the basement.
source_notes: Construction/completion dates, Adam Dome dimensions and thistle-frieze detail corroborated across Wikipedia and Old Edinburgh Club/SLHF sources.

name: The Balmoral Hotel
description: A red sandstone clock-tower landmark opened on 15 October 1902 as the North British Station Hotel, built directly above Waverley Station by the North British Railway to a design by William Hamilton Beattie. Its tower rises 190 feet, topped with four 13-foot clock dials made by Edinburgh jewellers Hamilton & Inches. Sean Connery renamed it The Balmoral during a major 1991 refurbishment, and Rocco Forte Hotels has owned it since 1997.
interesting_fact: The clock has run three minutes fast since it first started ticking in 1902, a deliberate trick to help travellers dashing for their train actually catch it - it's only ever set right once a year, at midnight on Hogmanay. J.K. Rowling finished writing Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows in room 552 here on 11 January 2007, later signing a marble bust in the room with the date and a line from the book. The hotel became the first in Scotland to earn a five-star Forbes Travel Guide rating, and past guests have ranged from Laurel and Hardy in 1932 to Oprah Winfrey in 2010.
source_notes: Architect, opening date, clock-tower height and the three-minutes-fast detail all corroborated across Wikipedia and Rocco Forte's own hotel history page. Deathly Hallows completion date/room number widely reported at the time.

name: Waverley Bridge
description: A wide iron-and-stone bridge built 1894-96 by engineers Blyth and Westland, carrying traffic across the deep valley between Princes Street and Market Street/Cockburn Street below - effectively forming the roof of Edinburgh Waverley station underneath it. Category A listed since 1991, it's one of three parallel crossings of this old loch-bed valley, alongside North Bridge and the Mound. Two carriageway ramps once let cars and taxis descend straight into the station concourse; that vehicle access was closed off in January 2014, leaving the ramps to pedestrians, cyclists and deliveries.
interesting_fact: Halfway across the bridge sits the station's former parcels office, itself Category A listed, converted into a pub and restaurant back in the 1980s - so crossing this bridge today can include stopping for a pint directly above the trains rumbling through the station underneath.
source_notes: Construction dates, engineers, listing status and 2014 vehicle-access closure corroborated via Wikipedia's Waverley Bridge article.

name: Edinburgh Waverley Station
description: Scotland's second-busiest railway station, formed in the 1860s when the North British Railway merged three separate rival Victorian stations that had grown up in this valley since 1846: the North Bridge, General and Canal Street stations. The combined name 'Waverley' had already been used informally from around 1854, borrowed from Sir Walter Scott's Waverley novels. Twenty platforms now radiate from a huge central island beneath a great glass roof, most recently reglazed with 370,000 square feet of clear panels between 2010 and 2012.
interesting_fact: A legal covenant dating back to the station's construction bans any building upward on the site, specifically to protect the view of Arthur's Seat from Princes Street above - one reason Waverley has always had to spread sideways and down into the valley rather than up, squeezed as it is between the Old and New Towns. Because it sits down in that valley, the station is almost entirely hidden from street level, with separate entrances dropping in from Waverley Bridge, Market Street and Princes Street on three different sides of the surrounding city blocks.
source_notes: Merger history, 'Waverley' naming and roof reglazing dates corroborated via Wikipedia and Network Rail's own history page. Used the Market Street-side Google Places result (closer to this leg's route) over the South Bridge concourse entry, both are the same station.

name: Waverley Market
description: A sunken plaza and shopping centre on the site of a Victorian fruit and vegetable market moved here in 1869 after the original marketplace under North Bridge was swallowed up by the growing railway. The Victorian market hall, roofed over in 1874 with an iron-and-glass structure and a rooftop garden used for entertainment, closed in November 1972 and was demolished the following year. The present shopping centre opened in November 1984, its roof deliberately built flush with Princes Street to preserve the classic view across to the Castle and Old Town, and was formally opened by the Queen on 25 July 1985.
interesting_fact: The centre has changed its name almost as often as its shop mix - Waverley Market, then Waverley Shopping Centre, then Princes Mall from 2004, then Waverley Mall from 2016 - before reverting back to its original name, Waverley Market, in a full-circle rebrand.
source_notes: Victorian market history, 1972 closure/1973 demolition and 1984/1985 shopping centre opening dates corroborated via Wikipedia's Waverley Market article. Name-change sequence (Princes Mall 2004, Waverley Mall 2016, reverted to Waverley Market) cross-checked against current 2026 signage/listings.

name: Fruitmarket Gallery
description: A contemporary art gallery occupying a building put up in 1938 as a genuine fruit and vegetable market, right beside the railway that once carried the produce in. Founded in 1974 and renovated by Richard Murphy Architects in 1994, it shows international and Scottish contemporary art free of charge, alongside talks and events. A £4.3 million expansion completed in 2021 converted a neighbouring former fruit warehouse - later the Electric Circus nightclub - into a second exhibition wing, roughly doubling the gallery's footprint.
interesting_fact: In 2011 the gallery commissioned artist Martin Creed to reclad the nearby Scotsman Steps in 104 different marbles sourced from quarries around the world - a free public artwork just a couple of minutes' walk from the gallery's own front door on Market Street, and one of Scotland's contributions to that year's Edinburgh Art Festival.
source_notes: Founding date, building history and 2018-2021 expansion corroborated via Wikipedia's Fruitmarket Gallery article; Scotsman Steps commission cross-checked against the gallery's own website.

name: Scotsman Steps
description: An enclosed stone staircase built between 1899 and 1902 inside an octagonal tower, linking North Bridge above down to Market Street and Waverley Station below - built at the same time as, and as part of, the grand new headquarters going up next door for The Scotsman newspaper. For decades afterwards the 104 steps were a dark, neglected shortcut, better known for litter and antisocial behaviour than for anything else.
interesting_fact: In 2011, Turner Prize-winning artist Martin Creed reclad every one of the 104 steps in a different marble drawn from quarries on every continent, a permanent public artwork titled Work No. 1059 and commissioned by the neighbouring Fruitmarket Gallery. Creed described climbing it as being 'like walking through the world' - and the £250,000 installation transformed the once-neglected passage into a genuine, free-to-visit piece of public art.
source_notes: Construction dates and Martin Creed installation details (2011, Work No. 1059, funding, 104 marbles) corroborated across Wikipedia and the Fruitmarket Gallery's own project page. name: The Scotsman Hotel
description: A dramatic Edwardian building completed in 1902 to designs by Dunn & Findlay as headquarters for The Scotsman newspaper, then Scotland's leading national daily. Built in pinkish sandstone with baronial turrets and ornate gables in a Scots Renaissance style, it was deliberately designed to command the skyline from its North Bridge position. Printing presses ran in the lower floors and editorial staff worked the middle ones, while - in a nod to older ways of getting news out fast - a pigeon loft once occupied the attic. Sitting right beside Waverley Station let finished papers reach the trains within minutes of coming off the press.
interesting_fact: The Scotsman finally moved out in 1999, and the building reopened in 2001 as a luxury hotel, keeping its oak-panelled Edwardian reception hall as a bar and turning the old basement printing-press room into a fitness suite - so guests now work out in the very room where the next day's headlines used to roll off the presses. A ceremonial staircase of Carrara marble still winds up through the building's core, unchanged from the newspaper's day.
source_notes: Architect, construction date (1899-1902) and conversion-to-hotel date (2001) corroborated across Wikipedia and Scotsman Publications' own retrospective coverage. Scots Renaissance/baronial architectural description and Carrara marble staircase detail from Edinburgh Architecture and hotel-review sources.

name: Jinglin' Geordie
description: A historic pub on Fleshmarket Close named after George Heriot, the wealthy 16th and 17th-century Edinburgh goldsmith and moneylender nicknamed 'Jinglin' Geordie' for the coins that jingled in his pockets as he walked the Old Town. Heriot lived on this very close with his first wife, Christian Marjoribanks, and lent substantial sums to King James VI and Queen Anne. Inside, the pub keeps a long-case clock, stained-glass thistle and saltire windows, and old prints and photographs of Edinburgh.
interesting_fact: When Heriot died in 1624 he left almost his entire fortune to found a hospital school for 'fatherless boys, freemen's sons of the town of Edinburgh' - that bequest became George Heriot's School, still one of Edinburgh's best-known independent schools today, funded by a goldsmith who once lived and worked just a few steps from where his namesake pub now stands.
source_notes: No dedicated Wikipedia article for the pub itself; George Heriot biography and 'Jinglin' Geordie' nickname corroborated across Edinburgh Expert, CAMRA and the pub's own venue history. George Heriot's School bequest is well documented independently.

name: Halfway House
description: Widely reckoned Edinburgh's smallest pub, tucked exactly halfway up the steep flight of steps that make up Fleshmarket Close between Market Street and Cockburn Street. The tiny bar counter fits no more than about four people at once, with a couple more tables and booths squeezed in around it, decorated throughout with railway memorabilia fitting for a pub standing this close to Waverley Station.
interesting_fact: Despite its size it punches well above its weight: CAMRA named it Scottish and Northern Ireland Pub of the Year in 2005 and Edinburgh Pub of the Year in 2009. It takes cask ale seriously too, with four handpumps of guest beers rotating daily alongside its own house-label Tullibardine malt whisky behind the bar. It now operates as part of the Old Town Pub Co, one of fifteen Old Town venues run by Bruce Group Scotland, though it still trades and is reviewed as a genuine free house rather than a chain outlet.
source_notes: No dedicated Wikipedia article; CAMRA awards (2005, 2009) and pub character corroborated across Forever Edinburgh, CAMRA branch listings and multiple pub-review sources. Current ownership (Old Town Pub Co / Bruce Group Scotland) confirmed via the operator's own website. User supplied a real exterior photo 2026-08-29, resolving the earlier no-image flag.

name: Fleshmarket Close
address: Market St & Fleshmarket Cl, Edinburgh EH1 1DE
description: A steep, narrow medieval alley climbing from Market Street, just behind Waverley Station, up to Cockburn Street and the High Street above. It takes its name from the flesh (meat) market once held here - butchers hung carcasses along the passage, with blood running down the slope toward the old Nor Loch that used to fill the valley now occupied by Princes Street Gardens. The market had moved here from beside the Tron Kirk by the late 17th century, and the close remains one of the most-used routes between the railway station and the Old Town today.
interesting_fact: It lent its name to Fleshmarket Close, the fifteenth Inspector Rebus novel by Edinburgh crime writer Ian Rankin, published in 2004, and long housed the Jinglin' Geordie pub, once a favourite haunt of journalists from the Evening News and The Scotsman until both papers moved out to Holyrood in 1999. More recently, in June 2025, the close was used to film J. J. Abrams's The Great Beyond, starring Glen Powell, Jenna Ortega, Emma Mackey and Samuel L. Jackson.

name: The Booking Office
description: The single-storey building at 17 Waverley Bridge began life as Edinburgh Waverley's original booking office, built by the North British Railway Company as the station was rebuilt through the 1890s. Passengers bought tickets here until the office became the station's parcels office around 1984, after which its timber-panelled counters were cleared out. Grade A listed and sitting directly above the station concourse - forming part of Waverley's own roof - the building later passed through spells as licensed premises and a restaurant before J D Wetherspoon opened The Booking Office here in March 2016.
interesting_fact: The pub's entrance floor carries a replica of the mosaic that once covered the real Victorian booking hall nearby, showing the North British Railway Company's coat of arms - the original, laid between 1892 and 1902, was ripped out with the old wood-panelled ticket counters in 1970. Photographs on the walls recall the station's steam-age heyday: the Flying Scotsman at the platform, 1945 refreshment trolleys, and the sleek 1960s Elizabethan express, alongside fragments salvaged from the very booking office the pub now occupies.

name: The Edinburgh Dungeon
description: The Edinburgh Dungeon occupies a Category B listed row of buildings at 31-39 Market Street, sunk down in the valley behind Waverley Station - a fittingly gloomy, half-underground setting for what's inside. Opened in 2000 by Vardon Attractions (now part of Merlin Entertainments, which also runs the original London Dungeon), it takes visitors through roughly 500 years of Scotland's darker history using live actors, sets and special effects rather than static displays - eleven shows and a ride, staffed by around fifteen actors, spread through the building's vaulted rooms.
interesting_fact: The cast of characters leans into Edinburgh's grislier past: Burke and Hare, the 1820s body-snatchers-turned-murderers who sold corpses to anatomists; Agnes Finnie, tried as a witch in 1644; and the legend of Sawney Bean, Scotland's supposed cannibal cave-dweller. The finale is the Drop Ride to Doom, a free-fall drop staged as a mock execution. A £500,000-plus refit in November 2016 rebuilt the Witch Hunt show around a new steel structure and an effects combination Merlin billed at the time as a world first for the format.

name: City Art Centre
description: A nine-storey iron-framed warehouse clad in restrained Beaux Arts stone, built 1899-1902 by architects Dunn and Findlay - the same firm and years as The Scotsman Hotel further up North Bridge - originally as an extension of the newspaper's works before it became part of Edinburgh's wholesale fruit and vegetable market. The City of Edinburgh Council converted it into a public gallery in 1980, a scheme by City Architect Brian Annable that won a RIBA Award for Architecture in 1983, and a 1990s expansion opened it out into six full floors of neutral, flexible gallery space.
interesting_fact: The council's own collection here runs to around 4,800 works of Scottish art from the 17th century to today - paintings, photography, sculpture and contemporary media by names like J.D. Fergusson, Joan Eardley and Eduardo Paolozzi - though with no permanent display, what's actually on the walls changes with each exhibition. A 1961 bequest from Edinburgh resident Jean Watson has quietly funded more than 900 acquisitions to the collection since, still shaping what turns up on show today.

name: Metal Thistle Sculpture
description: Officially titled 'Blawn Wi' The Wind' (Scots for 'Blown with the Wind'), this hand-forged thistle sculpture stands outside the Market Street Hotel at 6 Market Street. It's the work of blacksmith and metalwork artist Kev Paxton and his team at ArtFe, based in Ratho just outside Edinburgh, who built it from mild steel and reclaimed scrap - old farmers' fencing wire and parts salvaged from past exhibition stands among it - forged into Scotland's national flower caught mid-gust, its heads and leaves bent and rippling as though genuinely blown by the wind.
interesting_fact: After dark the sculpture is lit from below in purple LED, the thistle's traditional colour, making it glow against the surrounding stonework. Paxton has described the piece as a nod to the plant's old reputation for a 'don't mess with me' resilience - its spiked defiance standing in for courage and determination. Getting a permanently lit sculpture fixed into a public footpath inside a UNESCO World Heritage Site was its own undertaking: architects Leask, working alongside Paxton, had to navigate the 'complexities of consents, permits and logistics' the site demanded before it could go in.

name: Waverley Steps
description: This broad stairway down from Princes Street into Waverley station's concourse first opened in 1902, built alongside the North British Hotel next door - now the Balmoral - by the same North British Railway Company that owned them both. Flanked by original 1902 shopfronts to the east and Waverley Market to the west, the steps stayed largely unchanged for over a century until Network Rail rebuilt them in 2010-2012: a new escalator and lift were added for accessibility, all sheltered under a glass-and-steel canopy by Jefferson Sheard Architects, its frameless glass panels held up on branching steel 'tree' columns running down the centre of the stairs.
interesting_fact: Before the canopy, older Edinburgh residents remember the open steps as one of the windiest spots in the city centre - a funnel between the valley and Princes Street catching gusts from every direction. The £7 million rebuild had to satisfy tight heritage constraints: Waverley is a Grade A listed station inside a UNESCO World Heritage Area, so every part of the new structure needed sign-off before a single glass panel went up. The steps can still be gated shut at the top today, whenever the station closes for the night.
